region.en: Seashore of the unnamed city, Indian Ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 無名之城的海濱，印度洋（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 1 (1885), 'The Fisherman and the Jinni'

summary.en: A fisherman casts four times and draws up a copper jar sealed with the seal of Solomon; out of it rises a jinni who has sworn to kill whoever frees him. The fisherman tricks him back into the jar by asking how so huge a body could have come out of so small a vessel — and shuts the lid. The jinni bargains, and serves; and the fisherman, who would not open the jar a second time, tells the tale of the prudent man who believes a demon only once.
summary.zh: 漁夫四拋其網，撈起銅罐，上有素萊曼之印封；罐中升起妖靈，誓言必殺釋放他的人。漁夫以『如此龐大之軀如何出自如此小罐』之問誘其復入，蓋上蓋子。妖靈講條件而效力；不肯二次開罐的漁夫，講述只信魔鬼一次的智者的故事。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale (the Nights) belonging to the jinn lore of popular Islam; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A fisherman cast his net four times and drew up, the fourth time, a copper jar sealed with the seal of Solomon the son of David; and when he opened it there came out a jinni, huge as a cloud of smoke, who said: 'Now, that I have been a hundred years in the jar and no one came to free me, I swore in my anger to kill whoever should free me. Prepare to die.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), 'The Fisherman and the Jinni'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The fisherman said, 'Before I die, tell me: how could so huge a body come out of so small a jar?' The jinni stood and shook himself, and went back into the jar in a column of smoke; and the fisherman clapped the leaden lid upon it. 'Now choose thy death.' The jinni bargained, and swore by the Great Name to serve him if he let him out; and the fisherman let him out a second time only upon the oath — and the tale is told, the fisherman says, of the man who believes a demon once and no more.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, First Voyage: The Whale-Island

region.en: Indian Ocean trade route, whale-backed isle (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度洋商路，鯨背之島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The First Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: Sindbad lands with his shipmates on what they take for an island and cook their dinner on it; the island moves — it is the back of a mighty fish — and dives, and the crew are left to the sea. Sindbad alone is saved by a wooden trough of the king's, is carried to the capital, and made superintendent of the port; and he tells his tale on his return to the porter Sindbad of the city, who has groaned under his load all day.
summary.zh: 辛巴達與船友登上一座以為是島的陸地，在上面生火做飯；島動了——那是一條巨魚之背——潛入水中，船員盡落海。僅辛巴達靠木盆獲救，被帶至都城，任港口之監督；歸來時向終日負重的腳夫辛巴達講述他的故事。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Sindbad the sailor lands with his shipmates on what they take for an island — a green place, with a spring — and cook their dinner on it; and the island moves: it is the back of a mighty fish, and it dives, and the crew are thrown into the sea. Sindbad alone keeps hold of a great wooden trough that belongs to the king's supply-boat, and is carried on it to an island of the coast.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The First Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He is found there and carried to the capital, and made superintendent of the port; and on the strand he sees his own ship come in, with her crew, and recovers his goods. He returns to Baghdad rich, and tells his tale to the porter Sindbad of the city, who has groaned under his load all day; and the two Sindbads sit together in the evening, the bearer of burdens and the bearer of stories.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Second Voyage: The Valley of Diamonds and the Roc
title.zh: 辛巴達二次航行：鑽石谷與神鷹

region.zh: 楞伽島鑽石谷（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Second Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: Sindbad sleeps in a valley ringed by mountains where the diamonds lie on the bottom and the serpents keep the night watch, and merchants come to the rocks to throw down carcases for the eagles. He binds himself to a carcase, and the roc carries him up to her nest on the mountain-top, from which he comes down with a bag of diamonds and makes his way home to Baghdad.
summary.zh: 辛巴達眠於群山環繞之谷，谷底鑽石遍地，毒蛇夜巡；商人們來到崖頂拋下獸屍引鷹。他將自己縛於獸屍，神鷹將他帶上山頂的巢；他攜一袋鑽石下山，返回巴格達。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Sindbad is left on an island and sleeps in a valley ringed by mountains, where the diamonds lie on the bottom and serpents keep the night watch. Merchants come to the mountain heights and throw down carcases of beasts, which the eagles carry up to their nests; and the diamonds cling to the meat and are brought up with it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Second Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Sindbad binds himself to a great carcase with his turban, and the roc carries him up to her nest on the mountain-top; he fills his pockets and his turban with diamonds, and makes his way down to the merchants, and home to Baghdad with wealth beyond reckoning.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Third Voyage: The Giant of the Island

region.en: Island of the giant, eastern seas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 東海巨人島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Third Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: Shipwrecked, Sindbad's party reaches an island castle where a giant black eats the men one by one, roasting them on spits; the survivors blind him with two red-hot spits while he sleeps, and escape by raft — pursued to the shallows by stones. The tale is told as the oldest adventure of the East, cousin of Odysseus in the cave of the Cyclops.
summary.zh: 遇難後，辛巴達一行到達一島上城堡，黑色巨人逐一捕食眾人，於火上炙烤；倖存者趁其熟睡以兩支燒紅的烤叉刺盲其目，乘筏逃走——遭其擲石追至淺灘。此乃東方最古的冒險故事，為奧德修斯於獨眼巨人洞中之親緣。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the giant episode parallels the Odyssey's Cyclops; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Shipwrecked, Sindbad's party reaches an island castle where a giant black, tall as a palm, sits at the door; he seizes the men one by one, roasts them on spits and eats them. The survivors blind him with two red-hot spits while he sleeps, and he falls roaring down the stair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Third Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The men escape by raft and are pursued to the shallows by the stones of the giant's fellows; Sindbad alone is carried to another shore, where he is treated well by a merchant who loads him with aloes-wood for the market of Baghdad. He returns and tells the tale, and adds that every voyage cost him more than the last, and every tale was shorter than the truth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Fifth Voyage: The Old Man of the Sea

region.en: Indian Ocean, isle of the sea-ape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度洋海上老人之島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Fifth Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: A dwarfish old man with a face like an ape leaps on Sindbad's shoulders on the island shore and will not come off; he rides him for days, beating him with his heels, and drinks the water Sindbad brings him — the Old Man of the Sea. Sindbad carries a gourd of wine to the mariners' island, makes the sea-apes drunk, and loads a ship with their goods; and the Old Man rides no more.
summary.zh: 一貌似猿猴的侏儒老者躍上辛巴達之肩，不肯離去；他騎了他數日，以足跟夾擊，飲辛巴達取來之水——此即海上老人。辛巴達攜一葫蘆酒至海猿之島，使猿群醉倒，奪船載其貨而返；海上老人再不得騎人。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the Old Man of the Sea is one of the most quoted images of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: On the island shore a dwarfish old man with a face like an ape leaps on Sindbad's shoulders and will not come off; he rides him day after day, beating him with his heels, and drinks the water Sindbad fetches him — the Old Man of the Sea. The sailor carries him to the vines and squeezes grapes into his mouth, and at last the burden lightens.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Fifth Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Sindbad carries a gourd of wine to the island of the mariners, and the sea-apes drink and sleep, and he loads their ship with the goods of the dead crew. He escapes, and the Old Man rides no more; and the tale is the best known of the voyages, the picture of every burden a man carries that will not come off his back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Sindbad the Sailor, Seventh Voyage: The Last Return
title.zh: 辛巴達七航：最後的歸航

region.en: Eastern seas and Baghdad (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 東海與巴格達（象徵性定位於巴格達）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1885), 'The Seventh Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'

summary.en: On the last voyage the ship is wrecked on a coast of monkeys and pearls, Sindbad marries into the king's house, and learns the custom of the land: the husband is buried with the dead wife. He escapes from the grave of his wife by night, and lives for a while in the city of the buried living, until a ship takes him home — and he swears never to sail again. The seven voyages close with the formula: 'And I have recounted to thee, O my brother, all that befell me.'
summary.zh: 末次航行，船於猿猴與珍珠之岸遇難；辛巴達娶入王族，得知國俗：夫與亡妻同葬。他夜間自妻墓脫逃，於埋活人之城暫居，直至一船攜他歸家——他發誓不再航行。七次航行以慣用語收結：『兄弟啊，我已向你講完我的一切遭遇。』

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the buried-alive episode parallels descent narratives; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: On the last voyage the ship is wrecked on a coast of monkeys and pearls; Sindbad marries into the king's house, and learns too late the custom of the land: the husband is buried alive in the grave of the dead wife. He lies in the grave with the corpse, and escapes at night by the light of a fire kept at the mouth of the pit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885), 'The Seventh Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He lives for a while in the city of the buried living, and strips the graves as the others do; till a ship takes him home, and he swears never to sail again. The seven voyages close with the formula: 'And I have recounted to thee, O my brother, all that befell me' — and the two Sindbads, the bearer of burdens and the teller of tales, sit down together to the evening meal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 6 (1885); not verbatim.

region.zh: 巴格達底格里斯河岸（實際定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 1 (1885), 'The Three Apples'

summary.en: A fisherman draws up a chest from the river; inside is the body of a woman cut in pieces. The caliph Harun al-Rashid commands his vizier Ja'far to find the murderer in three days. The trail runs by a husband who bought three apples for his sick wife at a dinar each, a slave who mocked the purchase, a journey of murder and a journey of repentance — and ends with the slave's own cousin confessing to save the household, and the caliph's jest: 'I had thought to punish; instead I have bought a slave.'
summary.zh: 漁夫自河中撈起一箱；內有一被肢解的女子屍體。哈里發哈倫·拉希德限宰相加法爾三日內查明兇手。線索循一位曾以每枚一金幣為病妻買三個蘋果的丈夫、一位嘲笑其購買的奴隸、一次殺人之旅與一次懺悔之旅——終於奴隸之堂兄弟為保全家而自認，哈里發戲言：『本欲懲罰，結果買下一奴。』

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the murder mystery frame is one of the earliest detective narratives in world literature; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A fisherman draws up from the Tigris a heavy chest, and inside it the body of a woman cut in pieces. The caliph Harun al-Rashid commands his vizier Ja'far to find the murderer in three days, or die in his stead. Ja'far searches Baghdad in vain; on the last day the story is found at his own door, in the household of his own household's friend.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), 'The Three Apples'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The tale unravels from the murderer's own telling: a husband who bought three apples for his sick wife at a dinar each; a black slave who mocked the purchase and lied that he had had her love; the journey of murder; and the journey of repentance. A cousin confesses to save the husband, and the caliph's jest closes the case: 'I had thought to punish; instead I have bought a slave.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: The Hunchback's Tale: The Night of Four Guilty Tellers
title.zh: 駝背者的故事：四個自認兇手的夜晚

region.en: Kashgar to Cairo, road of the cycle (symbolic pin at Kashgar)
region.zh: 喀什噶爾至開羅的循環之路（象徵性定位於喀什噶爾）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 1 (1885), 'Tale of the Hunchback'

summary.en: A hunchback jester chokes on a fishbone at a tailor's supper; every host of the night believes himself the murderer — the tailor, the Christian broker, the Muslim steward, the Jewish physician, the barber of Kashgar and his brothers. Each buys off the dawn with the best story he can tell, and the barber, the last, revives the hunchback with a trick of the trade and the bone comes out. The tale is the great example of the story-cycle: five tales hung on one corpse.
summary.zh: 駝背弄臣於裁縫家晚宴上被魚刺哽死；當夜每一位主人皆自認是兇手——裁縫、基督徒經紀、穆斯林總管、猶太醫生、喀什噶爾理髮師及其兄弟。各人以最好的故事換取天亮；末位的理髮師以行當之技救活駝背人，魚刺取出。此乃故事循環之典範：五則故事繫於一具屍首。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the multi-narrator cycle is the Nights' signature device; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A hunchback jester chokes on a fishbone at a tailor's supper, and each host of the night believes himself the murderer — the tailor, the Christian broker, the Muslim steward, the Jewish physician of the town. Each buys off the dawn with the best story he can tell, and the tales are told in turn to the governor, who spares each teller for the sake of the tale.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885), 'Tale of the Hunchback'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The barber of Kashgar, last of the tellers, and the talker of six brothers, is brought in; he examines the dead man, feels his gullet, and draws out the bone with the instruments of his trade — and the hunchback revives. The tale is the great example of the story-cycle: five tales hung on one corpse, and a corpse that is not dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 1 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Nur al-Din Ali and Anis al-Jalis
title.zh: 努爾丁·阿里與蜜糖之光

region.en: Damascus and Baghdad (symbolic pin at Baghdad)
region.zh: 大馬士革與巴格達（象徵性定位於巴格達）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 2 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 2 (1885), 'Nur al-Din Ali and the Damsel Anis al-Jalis'

summary.en: The vizier of Damascus, dying, charges his son to bury his books with him and marry the daughter of a Cairene wazir. Nur al-Din Ali travels to Cairo, buys the singing-girl Anis al-Jalis for a thousand gold pieces, and is waylaid on the road home; the girl is taken to Baghdad and presented to the caliph, who will not take her — for she has told him whose she is. The lovers are restored, and the tale closes with the justice of the court.
summary.zh: 大馬士革宰相臨終，囑其子以書隨葬、娶開羅大臣之女。努爾丁·阿里赴開羅，以千金購歌女蜜糖之光（阿妮斯·賈利斯），歸途遇劫；女子被解至巴格達獻給哈里發，哈里發不肯納——因她告知其所屬。有情人得復聚；故事以宮廷之公義作結。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: The vizier of Damascus, dying, charges his son to bury his books with him and to marry the daughter of a Cairene wazir, and gives him a thousand gold pieces for her purchase. Nur al-Din Ali travels to Cairo and buys the singing-girl Anis al-Jalis, the light of sweetness; and on the road home the caravan is waylaid, and the girl is carried to Baghdad and presented to the caliph.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 2 (1885), 'Nur al-Din Ali and the Damsel Anis al-Jalis'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The caliph will not take her, for she has told him whose she is; and the tale closes with the justice of the court: the lovers are restored, the robbers are punished, and the two houses are joined by the marriage the dying father asked for.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 2 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Abu Kir the Dyer and Abu Sir the Barber
title.zh: 染匠阿布·基爾與理髮匠阿布·西爾

region.zh: 亞歷山大與伊斯坦布爾（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights core (Arabic, 8th-14th centuries); R. F. Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 7 (1885), public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 7 (1885), 'Abu Kir the Dyer and Abu Sir the Barber'

summary.en: Two neighbours of Alexandria — a cheating dyer and a generous barber — sail together to the capital. The dyer steals the barber's purse, has him branded a thief, and rises to be royal dyer by inventing colours no one knows; the barber washes in the hammam, is taken for a lord, and cures the king's scald-head with a salve of his own making. Justice is done at last at the table of the caliph; and the barber forgives the man who branded him — once.
summary.zh: 亞歷山大的兩位鄰居——行騙的染匠與慷慨的理髮匠——同船赴都城。染匠竊理髮匠錢袋，誣其為賊，並以發明無人知的顏色而晉升御用染匠；理髮匠於浴場洗浴，被誤為貴人，以自製藥膏治癒國王頭瘡。公義最終於哈里發席前得伸；理髮匠饒恕誣其之人——一次。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: Two neighbours of Alexandria sail together to the capital: Abu Kir the dyer, a cheat, and Abu Sir the barber, a generous man. The dyer steals the barber's purse, has him branded as a thief, and rises in the world by inventing colours no dyer has ever made; the barber washes in the hammam, is taken for a lord, and cures the king's scald-head with a salve of his own making.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 7 (1885), 'Abu Kir the Dyer and Abu Sir the Barber'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Justice is done at last at the caliph's table: the dyer is brought to account for the branding, and the barber, offered his enemy's blood, forgives him once — and the tale closes with the rule the barber keeps: forgive a man once; do not forgive him twice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Thousand Nights and a Night, vol. 7 (1885); not verbatim.

title.en: Abu Hassan, or the Sleeper Awakened
title.zh: 阿布·哈桑：醒來的沉睡者

region.zh: 巴格達哈里發宮（實際定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights Supplemental Nights (Arabic, medieval); R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain (Gutenberg #3446)

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 2 (1886), 'Abu Hassan, or the Sleeper Awakened'

summary.en: A broken merchant of Baghdad sleeps in the caliph's garden; Harun al-Rashid has him woken as the Commander of the Faithful, with a throne, a court and a purse — and, at evening, has him drugged and carried back to his own poverty. He wakes and cannot believe his year of power; and when the game is played a second time, he brings his wife, and the caliph's jest becomes the marriage of the household. The tale is the ancestor of every 'dream of the throne' told in the West since.
summary.zh: 巴格達一破產商人睡於哈里發花園；哈倫·拉希德命人以『信士長官』之禮喚醒他——寶座、廷臣與錢囊俱備——黃昏再以藥物使其昏睡，送回其貧舍。他醒來不信曾有掌權之年；第二次戲局時他攜妻同行，哈里發的戲言成全了這戶人家的婚姻。此故事為西方日後所有「王座之夢」敘事的先祖。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A broken merchant of Baghdad sleeps in the caliph's garden; Harun al-Rashid has him woken as the Commander of the Faithful, with a throne, a court, a purse, and a day of reign — and at evening has him drugged and carried back to his own poverty, where he wakes among his own debts and cannot believe his year of power.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886), 'Abu Hassan, or the Sleeper Awakened'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the game is played a second time he brings his wife, and the caliph's jest becomes the marriage of the household; and the tale is the ancestor of every 'dream of the throne' told in the West since — the man who has been king for a day and wakes to his old shoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886); not verbatim.

title.en: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves

region.en: Forest of the robbers, Persia of the tale (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 故事波斯的強盜森林（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the Galland cycle (18th c., from a Syrian storyteller); Arabic and French editions; R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 3 (1886), 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves'

summary.en: A poor woodcutter sees forty horsemen open a rock with the words 'Open, Sesame' and carries home a measure of gold. His rich brother Cassim goes, forgets the word, and is cut to pieces; the thieves return to find their cave betrayed, and hunt the household; and it is the slave-girl Marjaneh who outwits them — with the boiling oil in the oil-jars and the dance of the last thief — and marries the son of the house.
summary.zh: 窮樵夫見四十騎士以『芝麻開門』啟石入洞，帶回一量器黃金。其富兄卡西姆前往，忘卻口令，被剁成碎塊；群盜返洞察覺洩密，追索全家；機智的女奴瑪爾加娜以沸油灌罐、以及最後一盜之舞識破並剷除他們，嫁與家主之子。

sensitivity.note: A tale of the Galland cycle, of Syrian storyteller origin, now part of the Nights canon worldwide; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A poor woodcutter sees forty horsemen open a rock with the words 'Open, Sesame', and carries home a measure of gold on his three asses. His rich brother Cassim goes, forgets the word, and is cut to pieces at the door; his body is carried home sewn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 3 (1886), 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The thieves return to find their cave betrayed, and hunt the household; and it is the slave-girl Marjaneh who outwits them — she marks the doors, then marks every door alike, and in the hiding of the oil-jars she pours the boiling oil on the men hidden in them, and dances before the last of the thieves and kills him with the dagger in her girdle. She marries the son of the house, and the cave is left shut for ever.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 3 (1886); not verbatim.

region.en: City in China of the tale, and the Maghreb of the sorcerer (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 故事中的中國之城與術師的馬格里布（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Story of the Galland cycle (18th c., from a Syrian storyteller); Arabic and French editions; R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 6 (1888), 'Ala al-Din and the Magical Lamp'

summary.en: A lazy boy of the city is sent by an African sorcerer into a cave for a lamp; the boy keeps the ring, and the slave of the lamp builds him a palace overnight. The sorcerer returns, tricks the princess out of the lamp by crying 'New lamps for old!', and carries palace and bride to Maghreb; the princess drugs the sorcerer's cup, and the boy returns — and the palace is set back where it stood.
summary.zh: 城中懶童受非洲術師遣入山洞取燈；少年保住戒指，燈奴一夜為他建成宮殿。術師重返，以『新燈換舊燈』之喚騙走公主手中神燈，連宮殿與新娘一併攜往馬格里布；公主以藥下其杯，少年歸來——宮殿復歸原位。

sensitivity.note: A tale of the Galland cycle, of Syrian storyteller origin; the most retold story of the Nights; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A lazy boy of the city is sent by an African sorcerer into a cave for a lamp; the boy keeps the ring, and the slave of the ring brings him home; then the lamp is rubbed, and its slave builds him a palace overnight, with a garden of jewels and a marriage to the sultan's daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 6 (1888), 'Ala al-Din and the Magical Lamp'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The sorcerer returns in the dress of a lamp-seller, crying 'New lamps for old!'; the princess, who does not know the lamp's worth, gives it, and palace and bride are carried away to the Maghreb. The princess drugs the sorcerer's cup with the sleeping draught the boy brings her, and the boy returns, slays him, and has the palace set back where it stood.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 6 (1888); not verbatim.

region.zh: 波斯宮廷與君士坦丁堡（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Arabian Nights Supplemental Nights (Arabic, medieval); R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights, public domain

source.work: R. F. Burton, Supplemental Nights to the Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Volume 2 (1886), 'The Ebony Horse'

summary.en: A Persian craftsman brings to the king of Persia an ebony horse that flies wherever its rider turns the pegs. The prince rides it to the king of Constantinople's daughter, and the two are carried off into the air; the girl is stolen from the sleeping prince by a king of the islands, and the prince wanders the world in the dress of a pilgrim to find her again. The tale is the Nights' most famous story of the flying machine.
summary.zh: 波斯工匠向波斯王獻上一匹烏木馬，騎者轉動其釘即可飛行。王子乘之至君士坦丁堡王之女兒處，二人被帶上天空；女子於王子熟睡時被群島之王竊去；王子著朝聖者之衣浪跡天下尋她。此乃《夜》中最著名的飛行器故事。

sensitivity.note: Islamicate folk-tale of the Nights; the flying horse is shared with the Persian and Indian romance tradition; paraphrased from the public-domain Burton translation.

passages.text: A Persian craftsman brings to the king of Persia an ebony horse that flies wherever its rider turns the pegs in its neck. The prince rides it by night to the city of the king of Constantinople, and to the daughter of that king; and the two are carried off into the air together on the horse, and alight on a roof of the city.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886), 'The Ebony Horse'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The girl is stolen from the sleeping prince by a king of the islands, and the prince wanders the world in the dress of a pilgrim to find her again; the tale ends with the two restored, and the ebony horse returned to its maker — for the maker was the man who wanted the kingdom, and the flying machine was the price of the throne.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Burton, Supplemental Nights, vol. 2 (1886); not verbatim.
